newsitem.title: USA: Smoking increases risk of vision loss - study.
newsitem.headline: Smoking increases risk of vision loss - study.

text.p: Heavy cigarette smokers may run an increased risk of developing an untreatable eye ailment that causes progressive blindness, researchers said on Tuesday.

Two long-term studies of nurses and physicians found smokers face at least twice the risk of developing age-related macular degeneration, a disorder of the retina that causes an expanding area of blindness in the direct line of vision.

The disorder, the leading cause of new cases of blindness in those age 65 and older in the United States, begins with a partial breakdown of an insulating layer between the retina and the blood vessels behind it.

The effect on the macula, the area of the retina that distinguishes fine detail, is a circular area of blindness large enough to obliterate two or three words at normal reading distance. An estimated 1.7 million people are afflicted with it in the United States.

Researchers at the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary in Boston drew their conclusion from the Nurses Health Study, a 12-year look at 31,843 women who were between 50 and 59 in 1980 and whose health was checked over the years for a variety of conditions.

"Compared with women who never smoked, those who were smoking 25 or more cigarettes per day had 2.4 times the risk of (age-related macular degeneration), after adjustment for several other potential risk factors," study author Johanna Seddon and colleagues wrote.
Even those who quit smoking years earlier still had twice the risk of developing the eye problem, she said.

The study said the exact relationship between smoking and the disease was not known but theorized smoking may lead to it by affecting the blood flow to the eye or perhaps causing damage to the retina through oxidation.

A second team of researchers from Brigham and Women's Hospital and Harvard Medical School examined 21,157 male physicians over age 40 who were enrolled in the Physicians Health Study, a similar long-range program, and found a similar association between smoking and macular degeneration.

"The accumulated evidence adds yet another reason for not smoking cigarettes, namely, the possibility of developing an untreatable condition that causes blindness," Ronald and Barbara Klein of the University of Wisconsin Medical School wrote in an accompanying editorial.
"Physicians may be willing to go a bit beyond the data to suggest that not smoking may reduce the loss of vision and may ensure a brighter view of the world for years to come."
Both studies were published in this week's Journal of the American Medical Association.
